newsitem.title: INDIA: India moves to integrate local, global money markets.
newsitem.headline: India moves to integrate local, global money markets.

text.p: India's central bank has taken the first major steps to integrate the country's money and foreign exchange markets with the global market, bankers and analysts said on Wednesday.
"I think we are seeing the second stage of banking liberalisation," K. Kannan, chairman and managing director of state-run Bank of Baroda, told Reuters.
Kannan said the credit policy marked a step towards integrating Indian markets with international markets.

"We (authorised dealers in foreign exchange) have been allowed to borrow up to $10 million from our overseas offices," he said. "We can also invest an equal amount in overseas money market instruments."
This move could lead to an eventual alignment of Indian interest rates with international rates through arbitrage, Kannan said.
India's central bank unveiled its monetary and credit policy for first half 1997/98 (April-March) on Tuesday and reactions to the policy bordered on the euphoric.

The policy, welcomed by bankers and industrialists, gives greater freedom to banks to determine their own deposit rates, fix working capital loan limits to their borrowers and steps to integrate the foreign exchange, money and stock markets.
"Banks have been given great freedom, more than we expected," said M.S. Verma, chairman of State Bank of India (SBI), India's largest commercial bank.
"We have been given freedom in raising of deposits, in determining interest rates and in credit delivery," he said.
"The emphasis is now shifting on operational freedom to banks," Kannan said.
Bankers said the measures announced in the credit policy took banking reforms a logical step forward.

In the first stage of banking reforms, introduced in the early 1990s, the accent had been on cleaning up bank balance sheets by introducing prudential norms for income recognition, asset classification and provisioning for bad debts.
"Now that the bank balance sheets are more in line with international norms, we see a shift towards giving banks greater operational freedom," Kannan said.
Significantly, the policy also sought to ensure smooth flow of credit to industry while maintaining price stability, analysts said.

The twin objective of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) is to contain inflationary pressures without affecting adequate bank credit to support a real gross domestic product growth of 6.0-7.0 percent in 1997/98, central bank chief Chakravarty Rangarajan said in a letter to banks explaining the policy.
Rangarajan said slower expansion in M3 (money supply), targeted at 15.0-15.5 percent in 1997/98, should help keep inflation in check.
M3 grew by 15.6 percent in 1996/97 and real GDP (gross domestic product) is expected to have grown by 6.8 percent, the credit policy statement said.
Analyst Aashish Pitale of ICICI Securities and Finance Co said the policy aimed at ensuring smooth flow of credit to industry while ensuring price stability.

"Impediments in the credit delivery system have been removed," he said. "Banks have been told to plan credit deployment based on a projected increase in deposits of 800 billion rupees ($22.35 billion)."
This would take care of credit needs, he said.
"At the same time, the central bank is also keeping a close watch on inflation," Pitale said.
Rangarajan said the RBI had targeted an inflation rate of around 6.0 percent for 1997/98. Measured by the wholesale price index, year-on-year inflation was 7.35 percent for the week ended March 29.
